assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, with the magic-wavelength idea and fermionic strontium and ytterbium clocks, brought fractional uncertainties to the 1e-18 level. This is precision atomic physics at its best: a clear, original concept followed by a very large gain in accuracy. It opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice trapping scheme; Ye's JILA group drove the performance records and the comparisons. Two laureates is a clean configuration. Others (Lemonde, Bloom, Ludlow, Derevianko for theory) are in the periphery, but the core credit is fairly clear.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) have reproduced and improved the results, and the physics is stable. Timing is good, and the redefinition of the second adds weight.
uncertainties: The list credits only Katori and Ye, so whether the committee wants to pair this with ion-clock work or with comb-based metrology is open.
Part of the case rests on applications in metrology that are still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices act as clean, tunable quantum simulators of many-body models. The observation of the superfluid to Mott insulator transition is a conceptual landmark. The field has since produced single-site imaging and a large range of correlated phases. It speaks directly to fundamental understanding of many-body quantum mechanics.
assessment.attribution: The theory proposal (Jaksch, Zoller and colleagues) and the Munich experiment (Greiner, Mandel, Hänsch, Bloch) are the decisive steps; Esslinger's Fermi-Hubbard work and Cirac's simulation ideas are also strong. A three-person prize is possible but excludes deserving people. I chose the names I consider most central, with real uncertainty.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed across many groups for over twenty years, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is mature and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over five listed names, and any three leave out important contributors (Esslinger, Cirac).
Overlap with BEC (2001) and the trapped-ion work in B031 on Zoller and Cirac needs handling.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators opened a new class of matter characterised by a topological invariant and protected edge or surface states. Theory predicted it, and experiments confirmed it in HgTe quantum wells and in 3D materials. It is a major conceptual advance, and I judge it as an outsider to condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical proposal; Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang (not in the credited names) predicted the HgTe case and Molenkamp's group observed it. Hasan is credited for the first 3D observation but a three-person limit forces a choice. Credit is contested between spin Hall in 2D and 3D materials.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmations in several materials classes (HgTe, Bi2Se3 by ARPES) are strong, and the framework is well established. Recognition is timely, as it follows the 2016 topological-phase prize while being a distinct step.
uncertainties: The 2016 prize covered topological phases; the committee must judge how distinct this is.
Omission of Bernevig, Zhang or Hasan would be debated, and I defer to condensed-matter colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene turned a theoretical flat-band prediction into a platform with correlated insulators and superconductivity, and launched twistronics. It was an unexpected result in a very simple system and has produced a very large body of follow-up work.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated states and superconductivity in 2018. Andrei's group made related early observations, so the allocation is not entirely clear.
assessment.maturity: Many laboratories reproduced the effect within a few years, but sample dependence is a concern and some of the physics (pairing mechanism) is still under discussion. Recognition may be somewhat early but the discovery itself is solid.
uncertainties: The nature of the superconducting pairing is unresolved.
Credit for the experiments is shared with Andrei and others, and the sample variability is a known issue.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapped ions provide quantum gates and simulation with very high fidelity. The Cirac-Zoller proposal made quantum computation with ions concrete, and Blatt's group implemented gates and algorithms. It is a clear case where fundamental quantum control turned into a platform.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the gate scheme and Blatt's group did major demonstrations, but Wineland and the NIST group (and others such as Monroe) made decisive contributions, and Wineland was already recognised in 2012. That makes the fair allocation difficult.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups with improving fidelity, so the physics is well confirmed. Recognition could be seen as a continuation of 2012, and could come together with other quantum-information platforms.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with B021 and B020 on Zoller and Cirac.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for a platform to demonstrate clear advantage.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical objects of macroscopic size into the quantum regime, with ground-state cooling, squeezing and entanglement of motion. This speaks directly to the question of where the quantum-classical boundary lies, which I find compelling as a fundamental question.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg, Aspelmeyer and Painter each have decisive contributions (radiation-pressure cooling, strong coupling, ground-state cooling in nanostructures), but O'Connell and Cleland (not listed) and others also contributed to the quantum regime. Three names is plausible.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by several independent groups and platforms. The field is mature in terms of demonstrations, though practical impact is still emerging, and the question of a clear single discovery is open.
uncertainties: Not a single discovery but a field with several milestones.
Overlap with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum states.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter waves for exquisitely sensitive measurements of gravity, rotation and constants such as the fine-structure constant. It is a fundamental and precise application of quantum mechanics, though the discovery is more an invention than a discovery of something unexpected.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich all made foundational contributions (first atom interferometers, light-pulse formalism, precision gravimeters), while Chu (Nobel 1997) and Mlynek and Carnal also played roles. The three listed names are defensible.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated and applied. Impact is established in gravimetry, though the large-scale tests of fundamental physics are still in progress.
uncertainties: Credit is diffuse and overlaps earlier prizes (Chu, Cohen-Tannoudji).
Case rests on instrumentation as much as discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fractional charge and anyonic statistics reveal that quasiparticles in two dimensions need not be bosons or fermions. This is a fundamentally new form of quantum statistics, and recent interferometry and collider experiments have tested it directly.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim proposed the anyon concept in 1977, and Heiblum's group measured fractional charge. Wilczek, Laughlin and Halperin (not listed) are also essential, and the 1998 prize already recognised the fractional quantum Hall effect. Braiding experiments (Fève, Manfra) are recent.
assessment.maturity: Fractional charge is well established; direct anyonic braiding has been shown in recent experiments but is still being scrutinised. Premature for the statistics part, and mature for the charge.
uncertainties: Compound discovery: theory of anyons versus experimental confirmation come at different maturity.
Key theorists beyond the listed names are missing, which complicates a fair prize.
